extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy, psychology, and anyone interested in theories of humor and comedy
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizing and analyzing major philosophical and psychological theories of humor, their diagnostic features, techniques for producing jokes (e.g., set-up/punch), evolutionary accounts, ethical concerns, and affinities between comedy and philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority Theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Our laughter expresses feelings of superiority over other people or over a former state of ourselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classical lineage: Plato, Hobbes, Descartes; described as laughter that devalues its object (e.g., Roger Scruton: 'attentive demolition'). Explanatory claims: laughter as scorn or derision, often linked to moral objections (malice). Counterexamples and criticisms discussed (Hutcheson, Chaplin/Keaton film examples, self-directed laughter), showing superiority is neither necessary nor sufficient for all laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relief Theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter releases pent-up nervous or psychic energy—like a pressure-relief valve—so laughter is a discharge of superfluous energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical variants: Shaftesbury (animal spirits), Spencer (nervous energy discharged in non-instrumental muscular movements), Dewey (ending of suspense / relaxation of strain), Freud (detailed account in Jokes and Their Relation to the Unconscious). Freud distinguishes three laughter situations—der Witz (jokes/repartee), the comic (clumsiness, saving of cognitive energy), and humor (suppressed affect becomes superfluous and is released). The article notes empirical and conceptual criticisms of hydraulic/energy models and Freud's specific psychoanalytic claims, and gives examples (e.g., Harry Graham poem, Mark Twain story).

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity Theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter is caused by perceiving something incongruous—something that violates our mental patterns or expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lineage: Aristotle (expectation then violation), Beattie (incongruous united parts), Kant (sudden transformation of a strained expectation into nothing—laughter arises when expectation is dissipated), Schopenhauer (incongruity between abstract concepts and particular perceptions), Kierkegaard (contradiction/contrast between expected and experienced). Practical correlate: joke structure of set-up (creates expectation) + punch (violates it). The article discusses variations in what counts as 'incongruity' and notes that different theorists add incompatible details (e.g., Kant's 'transformation into nothing' vs. Schopenhauer's concept–perception gap).

rubrics_metrics.name: Set-up and Punch (expectation management technique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes often consist of a set-up that creates an expectation and a punch (line) that violates that expectation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly tied to Incongruity Theory and Aristotle's advice for speakers: the set-up establishes context/expectation; the punch delivers an unexpected ending that creates the incongruity. Examples: classical joke structures and how stand-up comedians frame and time set-ups and punches. The article uses this to explain many types of jokes (wordplay, misdirection, semantic shifts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Freud's three laughter situations (der Witz, the comic, humor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three distinct situations in which laughter functions as release: (1) der Witz (jokes/repartee) releases energy used for repression, (2) the comic releases surplus cognitive energy used in understanding, (3) humor releases affective energy prepared for but not expended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed psychoanalytic framing: der Witz involves bypassing censorship (sexual/hostile themes), the comic involves 'mimetic representation' and saved thinking-energy (e.g., clown clumsiness), and humor involves an expected affect becoming unnecessary (Mark Twain example). The article presents Freud's account and then critiques its empirical plausibility and theoretical oddities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity as concept–perception mismatch (Schopenhauer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor arises when there is a sudden perception of incongruity between an abstract concept and the real individual objects subsumed under it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer's formulation locates the incongruity specifically in the clash between conceptual/category-based thought and immediate perception (e.g., applying a general conception where a particular case defeats it). This explains certain forms of wit and also the offensiveness of being laughed at (exposes mismatch between conception and reality). Examples and implications for wit are given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kantian condition for laughter (strained expectation transformed into nothing)
rubrics_metrics.description: For lively convulsive laughter there must be something absurd: laughter arises from the sudden transformation of a strained expectation into nothing; the amusement is the play of thought producing bodily excitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant emphasizes that the expectation must be dissipated into nothing (not transformed into a positive opposite). He compares the pleasure in humor to the play in music and games of chance—rapid shifting of ideas produces bodily excitation. Examples: the Indian/ale story, other short anecdotes illustrating the sudden dissipation of expectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor as Play; Laughter as Play Signal (evolutionary/play theory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor and laughter evolved from mock-aggressive or rough-and-tumble play in apes; understanding humor as play explains many properties and benefits of humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The theory links laughter to play signals, suggests evolutionary functions (social bonding, practice for unexpected situations), and is used to counter traditional objections to humor by emphasizing its adaptive benefits. References to primate play research and evolutionary accounts are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Features distinguishing comic (non-painful) from tragic (painful)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ridiculous is a mistake or unseemliness that is not painful or destructive—the comic involves painless contradiction, whereas the tragic involves suffering contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawn from Aristotle and Kierkegaard: both tragic and comic are based on contradiction, but comic apprehension evokes a contradiction while indicating a 'way out' (painless). This distinction helps evaluate whether an instance is comedic or tragic and explains differing emotional responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical/moral evaluative criterion for humor (maliciousness and offensiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor can be morally objectionable when it involves malice, scorn, or ridicule that delights in another's self-ignorance or suffering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical critiques (Plato, early Christian writers, Puritans) view laughter linked to scorn, idleness, or vice; Plato and others argue comedy that humiliates or devalues should be controlled. Schopenhauer and Kant are appealed to for understanding why being laughed at offends. The article presents these ethical considerations as constraints or evaluative criteria when judging humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical criteria/affinities of standup comedy (seven features)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standup comedy shares affinities with philosophy; key features that characterize standup routines include being conversational, reflecting on familiar experiences, using questions to probe, emotional disengagement, critical thinking, careful attention to language, and delight in cleverness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List of seven affinities (as given): (1) conversational/interactive format; (2) reflection on familiar/puzzling experiences; (3) question-based probing; (4) emotional stepping-back/anesthesia of the heart; (5) critical, non-deferential approach; (6) attention to language and precision; (7) pleasure in clever, surprising thought. These serve both as descriptive criteria for what standup often is and as prescriptive guidance for producing philosophically-inclined comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive-two-stage processing (psychological models referenced)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some psychological models (e.g., Suls' two-stage model, cognitive-developmental analyses) describe humor appreciation as involving initial detection of incongruity followed by a benign resolution or reappraisal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the article truncates some of the psychology discussion, it references cognitive models (Thomas Schultz, Jerry Suls) that operationalize incongruity processing in stages (detection then resolution/benign appraisal). These function as processual criteria for when an incongruity becomes amusing rather than merely puzzling.
